title: My family
goal: Name the people in your family and say whose they are with mon, ma, mes, ton, ta, tes, son, sa, ses.

items.en: my, your, his/her: possessive words (mon/ma/mes, ton/ta/tes, son/sa/ses)

drills.en: Do you live with your parents?

drills.text: Raj habite à Toronto avec ___ fille. (his)
drills.en: Raj lives in Toronto with his daughter.
drills.explain: fille is feminine → sa, even though Raj is a man.

drills.prompt: How do you say “my friend Sofia” (Sofia is a woman)?
drills.explain: Before a vowel, French uses mon even with a feminine word: mon amie.

example.en: My mother lives in Québec City.

example.fr: Mon père parle arabe et français.
example.en: My father speaks Arabic and French.

items.note: Always plural here. In some contexts, les parents can also mean “relatives”.
œ is two letters joined (o + e). If your keyboard has no œ, oe is accepted.
Say [fis]: the l is silent and the s is pronounced. Same spelling in the plural: mes fils.
ma fille = my daughter; une fille = a girl.

example.fr: Raj habite à Toronto avec sa femme.
example.en: Raj lives in Toronto with his wife.

items.note: ma femme = my wife; une femme = a woman. Say it like “fam”.
un enfant (a boy, or a child in general), une enfant (a girl). Plural: les enfants, with liaison: mes‿enfants.
Same word for a man or a woman: le partenaire, la partenaire.

items.en: spouse or life partner (married or not)

example.fr: Ma sœur habite à Gatineau avec sa conjointe.
example.en: My sister lives in Gatineau with her partner.

items.note: Feminine: la conjointe. Very common in Canada, in everyday life and on official forms.

blocks.title: A coffee break at work in Montréal
blocks.context: Amira shows Olivier a photo on her phone.

lines.speaker: Olivier
lines.fr: Oh, c'est ta famille, sur la photo ?
lines.en: Oh, is that your family in the photo?

lines.speaker: Amira
lines.fr: Oui ! C'est mon mari, Karim. Et ça, c'est ma fille, Lina. Elle a huit ans.
lines.en: Yes! That's my husband, Karim. And that's my daughter, Lina. She's eight.

lines.speaker: Olivier
lines.en: And him, is he your son?

lines.speaker: Amira
lines.fr: Oui, c'est mon fils, Adam. Il a cinq ans.
lines.en: Yes, that's my son, Adam. He's five.

lines.speaker: Olivier
lines.fr: Et tes parents ? Ils habitent à Montréal aussi ?
lines.en: And your parents? Do they live in Montréal too?

lines.speaker: Amira
lines.fr: Non, mes parents habitent au Maroc, avec ma sœur. Mon frère habite à Toronto.
lines.en: No, my parents live in Morocco, with my sister. My brother lives in Toronto.

lines.speaker: Olivier
lines.fr: Moi, j'ai deux frères et une sœur. Ma sœur habite à Gatineau avec sa conjointe.
lines.en: I have two brothers and a sister. My sister lives in Gatineau with her partner.

lines.speaker: Olivier
lines.fr: Mes grands-parents habitent en France, à Lyon.
lines.en: My grandparents live in France, in Lyon.

blocks.body: Listen first. Notice the little words before each family word: [[mon]], [[ma]], [[mes]], [[ta]], [[tes]], [[sa]]. They all mean *my*, *your* or *his/her*. Why so many? That is this lesson.

steps.title: Family words and “my, your, his, her”

blocks.title: The family
head: French
English
blocks.note: Learn each word **with** its article: [[le]] for masculine, [[la]] for feminine, [[les]] for plural. [[L']] replaces le or la before a vowel.

blocks.title: My, your, his/her: the noun decides
blocks.body:
In English, *his* or *her* depends on the **owner**. In French, the possessive word agrees with the **person or thing owned**: is that noun masculine, feminine or plural?

- [[mon père]], [[ma mère]], [[mes parents]]
- [[ton frère]], [[ta sœur]], [[tes enfants]]
- [[son mari]], [[sa fille]], [[ses grands-parents]]

Use [[ton / ta / tes]] with someone you call *tu*. (The *vous* forms come later.)

blocks.title: Possessive words
head: masculine
feminine
plural
blocks.note: The plural form is the same for masculine and feminine: [[mes frères]], [[mes sœurs]].

blocks.title: son / sa = his OR her
blocks.pattern: son + masculine noun · sa + feminine noun · ses + plural noun
blocks.note: [[sa]] does **not** mean *her*, and [[son]] does **not** mean *his*. Look only at the noun that follows.

blocks.title: mon, ton, son before a vowel
blocks.pattern: mon / ton / son + feminine noun starting with a vowel
blocks.note: [[Ma amie]] is impossible to say smoothly, so French uses [[mon]], [[ton]], [[son]] instead, and links with a liaison: [[mon‿amie]]. The word itself stays feminine.

examples.en: Does your (female) friend live in Vancouver?

blocks.title: Presenting with c'est
blocks.note: [[C'est]] means *this is*, *that's* or *it's*. Perfect for photos and introductions.

blocks.body:
- **Copying English his/her:** Amira talking about her father says [[son père]], not [[sa père]]. Karim talking about his mother says [[sa mère]].
- **ma before a vowel:** say [[mon amie]], not [[ma amie]].
- **The English 's:** French has no *'s*. *Karim's wife* is [[la femme de Karim]]: “the wife of Karim”.
- **One son, two sons:** [[fils]] never changes: [[mon fils]], [[mes fils]]. Only [[mon]] / [[mes]] tells you how many.

- [[fils]] sounds like *feess*: silent l, pronounced s. [[fille]] sounds like *fee-y*.
- [[femme]] sounds like *fam*, not *fem*.
- [[mes]], [[tes]], [[ses]] all rhyme with *é*. Before a vowel, the s becomes a *z* sound: [[mes‿enfants]], [[ses‿amis]].
- [[frère]] and [[frères]] sound the same. In speech, you hear the difference only in [[mon]] (one) versus [[mes]] (several).

blocks.title: Partners in Canada
blocks.body:
[[Conjoint]] / [[conjointe]] is the everyday word for a partner in Québec, married or not. On Canadian immigration and tax forms in French you will see [[conjoint de fait]]: *common-law partner*.

In casual Québec French you will also hear (recognition only):

- [[mon chum]]: my boyfriend (or simply a male friend)
- [[ma blonde]]: my girlfriend, whatever her hair colour!

In France, people usually say [[mon copain]] / [[ma copine]] for boyfriend / girlfriend.

examples.en: This is my girlfriend, Sofia. (Québec, informal)
This is my boyfriend, Alex. (Québec, informal)

blocks.title: Listen and repeat
blocks.note: Repeat each line out loud, then record yourself and compare.

lines.fr: mon père, ma mère, mes parents
lines.en: my father, my mother, my parents

lines.fr: J'ai deux frères et une sœur.
lines.en: I have two brothers and a sister.
lines.tip: No liaison in deux frères: frères starts with a consonant.

blocks.explain: You hear [[mes]] (rhymes with é), so the noun is plural.
[[la femme de Raj]] = Raj's wife. Daughter is [[fille]], mother is [[mère]].

steps.title: Your turn
steps.intro: Answer without scrolling back. Getting something wrong now helps you remember it later.

blocks.prompt: Talking about Sofia's husband: “That's her husband.”
blocks.explain: mari is masculine, so son. Sofia being a woman does not matter.
optionFeedback: sa would match Sofia, but French looks at the noun: mari is masculine.

blocks.explain: parents is plural → mes; ils → habitent.

blocks.text: Raj habite à Toronto avec ___ femme et ___ enfants.
blocks.en: Raj lives in Toronto with his wife and his children.
blocks.explain: femme is feminine → sa; enfants is plural → ses.

blocks.prompt: Lina is talking about her friend Mei (a woman). Which is correct?
optionFeedback: Before a vowel, ma becomes mon: mon amie.

blocks.prompt: I have two brothers and a sister.
accept: J'ai deux frères et une sœur.
J'ai deux frères et une soeur.
blocks.explain: Use avoir for “have”; add -s to frères (silent).

blocks.prompt: My son is ten years old.
blocks.explain: Age uses avoir: [[il a dix ans]]. fils is masculine → mon.
Listen for the liaison in [[mes‿enfants]] and the accent in [[à]].

blocks.en: Lucie, do you live with your partner?
blocks.explain: You're talking to Lucie with tu → ton; conjoint is masculine.

blocks.prompt: Imagine you are showing a family photo to a colleague. Present three or four people: who they are, where they live, and maybe their age.
checklist: Where one person lives: il / elle habite à …
One age: il / elle a … ans
Use mes for a plural (mes parents, mes enfants…)

models.label: Model answer
models.fr: Alors, c'est ma famille. C'est ma femme, Priya. Et ça, c'est mon fils, Arjun. Il a dix ans. Mes parents habitent en Inde, et ma sœur habite à Vancouver avec son mari.
models.en: So, this is my family. This is my wife, Priya. And that's my son, Arjun. He's ten. My parents live in India, and my sister lives in Vancouver with her husband.

blocks.prompt: Write about your family in 4–5 short sentences: who is in your family, where they live, and how old one or two people are.
checklist: Use mon, ma and mes correctly
Use son, sa or ses at least once
Say where someone lives (habiter à / en / au)

models.label: Model answer
models.fr: Je m'appelle Raj. J'habite à Toronto avec ma femme et mes deux enfants. Mon fils a dix ans et ma fille a six ans. Mes parents habitent en Inde. J'ai une sœur. Elle habite à Vancouver avec son mari.
models.en: My name is Raj. I live in Toronto with my wife and my two children. My son is ten and my daughter is six. My parents live in India. I have a sister. She lives in Vancouver with her husband.

summary:
- Name your family: [[le père, la mère, le frère, la sœur, le fils, la fille, le mari, la femme, les enfants, les grands-parents]]
- Say *my, your, his/her* with [[mon/ma/mes, ton/ta/tes, son/sa/ses]], matching the noun, not the owner
- Use [[mon]] before a feminine word starting with a vowel: [[mon amie]]
- Present people with [[C'est ma sœur]] and [[J'ai deux frères]]
